Job of the Week: Lead Buyer, IT

This week I'm working with a defence prime that is growing its IT procurement team, and they're hiring several Lead Buyers. The team covers enterprise and engineering software, SaaS, cyber, networks, hardware, AI, and high-performance computing across the UK and Europe.

There are two ways into the team.

1. Lead Buyer, IT Category (£45k to £55k)
For an IT Buyer ready to step up, or an Indirect Buyer who already has an interest in technology and wants their first move into IT procurement. You'll run large sourcing projects in support of the Category Managers, with room to specialise in one area and grow into others over time.

2. Lead Buyer, IT Transformation (£50k to £60k)
For a procurement lead who has run complex, strategic projects or programmes. It's a high-profile business transformation programme, and you'll lead the procurement side from start to finish: RFI/RFP, SOWs, contracts, SRM and supplier performance. It sits in IT, but they'll look at any procurement background if you've delivered at this level.

What the roles share
-Can be based in either Stevenage or Bolton, hybrid with 2 to 3 days a week on site
-International work, with quarterly team meetings that rotate between the UK, Germany, Italy and France
-Support towards MCIPS if you're not already there
-Bonus, up to 14% combined pension, paid overtime, up to 15 extra flexi days

Due to security clearance requirements, you will need to hold current British citizenship to be able to be considered.

These roles suit people who like building relationships across countries and owning a project end to end, not just processing POs.

If this sounds like you, or you're curious but not actively looking, drop me a message to find out more. And if you know a good buyer who's been sitting in the same seat too long, please send this their way.

The most persistent blind spot I see in GitOps is the assumption that it is only about applying YAML to Kubernetes clusters. In 2026, that framing is dangerously outdated. GitOps has become the decision audit trail for cloud infrastructure, and the teams still thinking in terms of manifests and sync waves are the ones getting blindsided.

The non-obvious shift is that GitOps is no longer just a deployment strategy. It has become the central nervous system for autonomous infrastructure operations. The latest industry data confirms that by 2026, GitOps extends far beyond Kubernetes. Pull requests are now the centerpiece for everything: infrastructure changes, security policy updates, automated validation, and AI-driven remediation. The winning teams are not the ones with the fastest Argo CD syncs. They are the ones that have designed their GitOps workflows so that every change, whether human-generated or AI-proposed, must pass through a pull request that enforces cost guardrails, compliance checks, and observability hooks before it ever touches production.

Another blind spot most platform teams miss is the rise of bidirectional GitOps. The common perception is that GitOps is a one-way sync from Git to infrastructure. The reality in 2026 is that the best platforms now reconcile changes made directly in the cloud back into the Git repository, creating a true source of truth that prevents drift. The teams that are winning are the ones that have embedded this reconciliation into their observability loop, so they can answer the question "did this manual override break the intended state" within seconds, not days.

For hiring managers and recruiting leaders: I do not just set up Argo CD or Flux. I design GitOps architectures that are built for autonomous operations, where the pull request is the governance contract between the operator and the business. I understand that GitOps in 2026 is not a tool you install. It is an operational model that requires designing the policy enforcement layer, the drift detection feedback loop, and the rollback strategy before the first repository is connected. If your team is struggling with AI-generated infrastructure changes that bypass manual review, cloud drift that creates silent inconsistencies, or a GitOps setup that cannot correlate a deployment with a business outcome, I can architect the solution.

The hardest question nobody is asking: When an AI agent opens a GitOps pull request at 3AM to remediate a detected security vulnerability, and that change passes every automated validation but introduces a subtle cost increase that only appears 48 hours later due to a misconfigured autoscaler, who is accountable for that tradeoff, and how do you audit the decision in the merge commit?

The global population is not simply “shrinking.”

But the workforce is changing — and not in the same way everywhere.

In many higher-income economies, populations are aging and working-age talent pools are beginning to contract.

At the same time, younger workforces continue to expand across other regions.

For technology companies, this creates a new challenge:

How do you keep building when the skills you need are no longer available in one location?

Here is what the demographic shift could mean for tech:

1️⃣ Competition for specialized skills will intensify

As experienced workers retire and fewer younger workers enter some labour markets, companies may face stronger competition for engineers, AI specialists, cybersecurity professionals, data experts, and technical leaders.

2️⃣ Automation will become a capacity strategy

AI and automation will not only be used to reduce costs.

They will help smaller teams handle repetitive work, improve productivity, and focus human expertise on decisions that require context, creativity, and accountability.

3️⃣ Products will need to serve older users

Aging populations will increase demand for accessible digital products, health technology, assistive tools, financial services, and interfaces designed for a wider range of physical and cognitive needs.

4️⃣ The workforce will become more age-diverse

Companies will need better systems for retaining experienced professionals, supporting continuous learning, and helping workers adapt as technologies and required skills change.

5️⃣ Talent strategies will become more global

When expertise is scarce locally, companies will increasingly need to recruit across regions, build distributed teams, and access specialists without requiring relocation.

6️⃣ Knowledge transfer will become business-critical

As senior professionals leave the workforce, undocumented technical and institutional knowledge can disappear with them.

Strong documentation, mentoring, succession planning, and structured handovers will become essential infrastructure.

The future is not simply about doing the same work with fewer people.

It is about combining human expertise, AI, automation, continuous learning, and global talent more effectively.

The companies that prepare early will not be limited by the size of one local hiring market.

They will build access to the skills they need — wherever those skills are located.

Is your talent strategy prepared for demographic change?

Or is it still built around an unlimited local supply of candidates?

The cost of building has collapsed to near-zero, historically speaking.

Twenty years ago, starting something meant hiring a dev team, buying servers, doing your own design, writing your own copy, maybe even your own legal docs. That's capital + time + a team just to get to idea validated in the market. Now one person with AI tools can build a working product, write the marketing copy, generate the logo, debug the code, and draft the contract — solo, in a fraction of the time. The barrier that used to filter out 90% of "wantrepreneurs" basically dissolved.

But here's the layer under that — it's not really about AI, it's about what happens whenever a barrier collapses in history.

Same pattern happened with:

- The printing press → suddenly everyone could be a "publisher," pamphlets exploded, most were garbage, a few changed the world. 
- YouTube/cheap cameras → everyone became a "filmmaker/creator," 99% noise, but it also produced entire new industries nobody predicte. 
- No-code website builders (2010s)→ sudden explosion of "agencies" and micro-SaaS, most died, some became real businesse. 

The actual mechanism: when the cost of attempting something drops, the number of attempts explodes, but the success rate per attempt usually drops too — because the barrier wasn't just filtering out capital-poor people, it was accidentally filtering out people who weren't serious enough to push through friction. Remove the friction, and you get flooded with people who wouldn't have survived the old gauntlet.

The genuinely fascinating part: this means we're in a very temporary window. Right now, *having* an AI-assisted MVP is still slightly impressive because most people haven't caught up. In a few years, everyone will have one — the differentiator quietly shifts from "can you build it" (which used to be the moat) back to the boring stuff that never went away: distribution, positioning, actually solving a real pain point, and not quitting when it's hard. The tools changed. The thing that actually separates who wins didn't.

Kind of ironic that the AI era, which makes building trivial, ends up proving that building was never the hard part.

BigLaw associate with documented AI workflow skills is now earning $28,000-$41,000 more than a peer at the same level without them. That gap widened 31% in a single year. None of these job titles existed when most of us were choosing a career path.
 
I keep getting asked "how do I get into legal tech" like it's one job. It isn't. It's a stack — and knowing which layer you're aiming for changes everything about what to learn.
 
Legal tech runs on roughly four layers, and a distinct job family is forming at each one:
 
The data layer is the foundation — case law, contracts, filings, internal matter history. This is where Legal Knowledge Analysts and Legal Knowledge Engineers live, cleaning and structuring the material everything above it depends on.
 
The AI reasoning layer is where models actually process legal language. Legal Engineers and Legal AI Trainers/Prompt Engineers sit here — half technologist, half domain expert, tuning how the system interprets legal text.
 
The verification layer connects AI output back to real, citable sources — the part that stops a model from confidently making things up. AI Governance and Data Privacy specialists increasingly own this, because verification and compliance turned out to be the same problem.
 
The workflow layer is where it all meets the humans who actually use it — Legal Operations, Contract/CLM Specialists, and Legal Tech Product Managers, wiring AI into case management, billing, and intake systems lawyers touch every day.
 
The growth is real and it's not just a US story. India alone has 800+ active legaltech companies, courts are sitting on more than 5 crore pending cases, and the Supreme Court's draft AI judiciary policy is expected to accelerate hiring further. Legal ops is the fastest-growing entry point; product management is the highest-paid trajectory.
 
On pay: entry-level Indian legal tech roles run ₹4-12L depending on track, mid-level ₹9-25L, and senior/lead roles clear ₹25-50L, with product management and AI governance roles topping that range. In the US, 67% of employers now pay more for AI skills specifically — not general tech skills, AI skills — and in-house legal ops candidates with verified AI experience get offers averaging 19.3% higher.
 
What to actually learn depends on which layer you're chasing. Law-first roles still need contract expertise and process mapping — but now paired with data literacy and workflow tools. Tech-first roles need CLM platforms, prompt design, and no-code automation — but they don't work without real legal domain grounding. The people getting hired fastest aren't purely lawyers or purely engineers. They're the ones who can stand at the layer boundary and translate.
 
You don't need to become an AI engineer to build a career here. You need to know which layer you actually want to sit in.
 
Which layer are you building toward — data, reasoning, verification, or workflow?

We're losing the human-to-human negotiation that builds deals.

I believe AI should amplify us. Not complicate trust. Not replace the handshake. Not turn every deal into a legal chess match where neither side knows if they're talking to a person or a prompt.

How do we keep the human at the center when AI is in the room?

Your AI agent finished the task. Another AI graded it: PASS.

They can both be wrong.
So who checks the checker?
Generation got cheap.
Verification did not.

The old bottleneck was completing the task.
The new bottleneck is knowing whether the result is right.

Giving the model a confidence score is not verification.
Using a second model as a judge helps—but it does not make the judgment neutral.

A reliable evaluation system uses layers:
Deterministic checks for contracts, schemas, permissions and exact outcomes.

A calibrated LLM judge for fuzzy quality, guided by a written rubric and compared with expert labels.

Human judgment where context, ambiguity or consequences matter.

Production evidence to expose failures the original evaluation set missed.
This changes the role of QA.

QA is not the person manually checking every AI response.

QA becomes the person who:
defines what “correct” means;
identifies what must never break;
creates the golden data set;
chooses the right graders;
calibrates model judges against humans;
investigates failures and non-determinism;
sets release thresholds based on risk.

One distinction matters:
Evals measure behaviour.
Guardrails constrain live actions.
Humans own risk and escalation.
If an agent passes 96% of its evals, the critical issue is not the 96%.

It is whether the remaining 4% contains something you cannot afford to break.
Confidence is a claim. Evidence earns trust.

We are hiring 4 x ASIC contractors on behalf of our customer 💡📢

The company is a seed-stage well funded San Francisco based startup applying modern AI to silicon’s biggest bottleneck: analog. We have openings for contract circuit and layout designers. The work is remote: we provide the machines, PDKs and EDA licenses. Start dates are project-based, starting now, with room to extend.
 
1. Analog/ Mixed-Signal Circuit Design (2 openings)
 
Design and verify high-speed ADCs and the analog front ends of ADC-based SerDes receivers in advanced FinFET nodes.
Typical blocks: SAR and time-interleaved SAR ADCs, comparators, sampling front ends and track-and-holds, reference and bias circuits, clock distribution and timing-skew calibration, CTLE/AFE and termination.
Looking for: industry tape-outs of high-speed ADCs or SerDes receivers in FinFET, plus hands-on transistor-level design and simulation through signoff, including post-layout. Cadence or Synopsys flows are both fine.
 
2. Analog/ Custom Layout Design (2 openings)
 
Lay out high-speed data converters and SerDes analog blocks in advanced FinFET nodes.
Typical work: matched and interleaved arrays, common-centroid and symmetric placement, high-speed clock and signal routing, parasitic-aware layout, EM/IR, and DRC/LVS signoff.
Looking for: industry tape-outs of ADC or SerDes layout in FinFET. Virtuoso or Custom Compiler experience is fine.
